items.stem: The peace conference was dominated by the “Big Three”: Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Wilson. What were Clemenceau's aims at the Paris Peace Conference?
items.answer: He wanted France to be secure from future German attack. He wanted Germany's army and industry weakened. He wanted the Rhineland separated from Germany or controlled as a buffer. He wanted Alsace-Lorraine returned to France. He wanted large reparations to rebuild the devastated north-east of France.

items.stem: The peace conference was dominated by the “Big Three”: Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Wilson. (a) What were Wilson's aims at the Paris Peace Conference? [4] (b) Why did Wilson want a fair treaty with Germany? [6]
items.answer: (a) He wanted a peace based on the Fourteen Points. He wanted self-determination for the peoples of eastern Europe. He wanted a League of Nations to keep the peace. He wanted Germany punished but not so harshly that it would seek revenge. He wanted disarmament, free trade and freedom of the seas. (b) The USA had suffered far less than France and did not want revenge. He believed a harsh treaty would make Germany seek revenge and cause another war. He wanted the peace to be based on justice and the Fourteen Points. He wanted a strong, democratic Germany as part of a League of Nations.

items.stem: The peace conference was dominated by the “Big Three”: Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Wilson. (a) What were Lloyd George's aims at the Paris Peace Conference? [4] (b) Why did Lloyd George find it difficult to achieve his aims? [6]
items.answer: (a) He had promised British voters in December 1918 that Germany would pay. He wanted to end the threat of the German navy to Britain. He wanted to protect and extend the British Empire, for example by taking German colonies. He wanted Germany to recover so it could trade with Britain. He feared a harsh peace would cause German revenge or a communist revolution. (b) He had promised British voters he would “make Germany pay”, so he could not seem soft. He privately wanted a moderate peace so Germany could trade and not seek revenge. Clemenceau demanded far harsher terms. Wilson's ideas such as freedom of the seas conflicted with British interests.

items.stem: The peace conference was dominated by the “Big Three”: Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Wilson. ‘Clemenceau's aims were the most reasonable of the Big Three.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: France had suffered the greatest losses and devastation among the Big Three. France bordered Germany and had been invaded twice in fifty years, so security was a real need. Against: Wilson's aims looked further ahead to a lasting peace. Lloyd George understood that a crippled Germany would harm European trade and stability. A very harsh peace risked German revenge. Judgement: Clemenceau's aims were understandable given France's losses and position, but Lloyd George's and Wilson's concern for lasting stability made their aims more realistic in the long term.

items.stem: The peace conference was dominated by the “Big Three”: Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Wilson. How far did the Big Three agree about how Germany should be treated? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: All agreed Germany should be punished in some way, disarmed and lose some territory. All agreed Alsace-Lorraine should go back to France and that Belgium should be restored. Against: Clemenceau wanted Germany crippled; Wilson wanted a just peace. Lloyd George wanted Germany to recover as a trading partner. They clashed over the Rhineland, the Saar, reparations and freedom of the seas. Judgement: They agreed on the general principle of punishment but disagreed sharply about its extent, which is why the treaty was a compromise.

items.stem: The Treaty of Versailles was a compromise between the very different aims of the Big Three. (a) Describe what Clemenceau achieved at the Paris Peace Conference. [4] (b) Why was Clemenceau criticised in France after the treaty was signed? [6]
items.answer: (a) Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France. The Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by Allied troops for 15 years. France gained control of the Saar coal for 15 years. Germany's army was limited to 100,000 men. Germany accepted war guilt and had to pay reparations. (b) Many French people believed the treaty was too soft on Germany. France did not gain the Rhine as its frontier or a separate Rhineland state. The Saar was only controlled for 15 years. The Anglo-American guarantee of French security collapsed when the US Senate rejected the treaty.

items.answer: For: Clemenceau did not get the Rhineland separated and was voted out of office in 1920. Wilson saw the US Senate reject the treaty and the League. Judgement: Each leader gained important aims, but none was fully satisfied; the treaty was a compromise that each could defend only in part.

items.stem: Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory under the Treaty of Versailles. ‘Reparations were the most important reason why the Germans hated the Treaty of Versailles.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: £6,600 million was seen as a crushing burden that would last for generations. Reparations led directly to the Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation in 1923. Against: War guilt (Article 231) was seen as a lie and a national humiliation. Being forced to accept a diktat without negotiation caused deep resentment. Loss of territory and people, such as the Polish Corridor, angered nationalists. Disarmament left Germany feeling defenceless. Judgement: Reparations caused the most practical hardship, but war guilt and the diktat explain the depth of resentment, because reparations were justified by the war guilt clause.

items.stem: In January 1919 the leaders of the victorious powers met in Paris to draw up the peace settlement. What were Clemenceau's aims at the Paris Peace Conference?
items.answer: He wanted France to be secure from future German attack. He wanted Germany's army and industry weakened. He wanted the Rhineland separated from Germany or controlled as a buffer. He wanted Alsace-Lorraine returned to France. He wanted large reparations to rebuild the devastated north-east of France.

items.stem: In January 1919 the leaders of the victorious powers met in Paris to draw up the peace settlement. (a) What were Clemenceau's aims at the Paris Peace Conference? [4] (b) How far did the Big Three agree about how Germany should be treated? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) He wanted France to be secure from future German attack. He wanted Germany's army and industry weakened. He wanted the Rhineland separated from Germany or controlled as a buffer. He wanted Alsace-Lorraine returned to France. He wanted large reparations to rebuild the devastated north-east of France. (b) For: All agreed Germany should be punished in some way, disarmed and lose some territory. All agreed Alsace-Lorraine should go back to France and that Belgium should be restored. Against: Clemenceau wanted Germany crippled; Wilson wanted a just peace. Lloyd George wanted Germany to recover as a trading partner. They clashed over the Rhineland, the Saar, reparations and freedom of the seas. Judgement: They agreed on the general principle of punishment but disagreed sharply about its extent, which is why the treaty was a compromise.

items.stem: None of the peacemakers went home from Paris with everything they wanted. How far did Wilson achieve his aims at the Paris Peace Conference? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The League of Nations was written into the treaty. New states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia reflected self-determination. Against: The treaty was much harsher on Germany than he wanted. Disarmament and freedom of the seas were not achieved. The US Senate rejected the treaty, so the USA did not join the League. Judgement: Wilson achieved his central aim of the League and some self-determination, but his failure at home undermined much of what he gained.

items.stem: A student writes: “The Treaty of Versailles left Germany with no army at all.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. Germany was allowed an army of 100,000 men, but no conscription, tanks or air force.

items.stem: What were the military terms of the Treaty of Versailles?
items.answer: The army was limited to 100,000 men. Conscription was banned. Germany was not allowed tanks, an air force or submarines. The navy was limited to six battleships. The Rhineland was demilitarised.

items.stem: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors. Describe the territorial terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
items.answer: Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France. West Prussia and Posen went to Poland, creating the Polish Corridor. Danzig became a Free City under the League. The Saar was run by the League for 15 years. Eupen and Malmedy went to Belgium and North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite. Germany's colonies became League mandates.

items.stem: Separate treaties were made with Germany's allies: Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey. Describe how the treatment of Turkey changed between the treaties of Sèvres and Lausanne.
items.answer: Sèvres gave Smyrna and Eastern Thrace to Greece, but Lausanne returned them to Turkey. Sèvres put the Straits under international control; at Lausanne they stayed Turkish but demilitarised. Lausanne removed the military restrictions and reparations of Sèvres. Both confirmed the loss of the Arab lands, which became British and French mandates.

items.stem: In 1919 J. M. Keynes, a British economist, attacked the Treaty of Versailles as unjust. Describe the arguments used at the time to justify the Treaty of Versailles.
items.answer: Germany had imposed the harsh Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on Russia in 1918. Northern France and Belgium had been devastated and needed rebuilding. Victorious governments faced public demands to punish Germany. Germany kept most of its land and its industrial strength. Disarmament aimed to prevent future German aggression.

items.stem: How far was the Treaty of Versailles a “Carthaginian peace”? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Germany lost land, colonies, its air force and most of its navy. War guilt and reparations were seen as humiliating and crippling. Against: Germany was not occupied or divided and kept most of its population and industry. Reparations were reduced and only partly paid. Germany recovered quickly in the late 1920s. Judgement: The treaty was harsh in tone and in some terms, but it fell far short of destroying Germany, so “Carthaginian” overstates it.

items.stem: The peace conference was dominated by the “Big Three”: Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Wilson. What were Lloyd George's aims at the Paris Peace Conference?
items.answer: He had promised British voters in December 1918 that Germany would pay. He wanted to end the threat of the German navy to Britain. He wanted to protect and extend the British Empire, for example by taking German colonies. He wanted Germany to recover so it could trade with Britain. He feared a harsh peace would cause German revenge or a communist revolution.

items.answer: (a) To persuade Clemenceau and Wilson to moderate the terms, especially on territory and reparations. Context: By March 1919 the Big Three were deadlocked over the Rhineland and reparations. (b) Useful: Lloyd George warns that a treaty Germany sees as unjust will lead to German revenge, however weak Germany is made. Provenance: it is a private paper by Lloyd George himself, so it shows his real view rather than his election promises. Limitations: it was written to influence the other leaders, so he may have exaggerated the danger. It does not show: That Lloyd George had publicly promised British voters to make Germany pay.

items.stem: Describe the effects of the occupation of the Ruhr in 1923.
items.answer: German workers went on strike in passive resistance. French troops took over mines and factories and some workers were killed. Industrial production in Germany fell sharply. The government printed money to pay striking workers. This made inflation spiral into hyperinflation.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Germany paid the full £6,600 million of reparations in the 1920s.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge. (b) A revision website states: “Brest-Litovsk shows that Germany was treated more harshly than it had treated others.” Is this accurate? items.answer: (a) Not accurate. Payments were reduced by the Dawes (1924) and Young (1929) Plans and ended in 1932; only a fraction was paid. (b) Not accurate. Brest-Litovsk took about a third of Russia's population and much of its industry, which defenders of Versailles used to argue the opposite.
